Speaking as I would in that garden, I’d start by softening the frame a bit. What feels “unconventional” to one person is just ordinary life to someone else. So the baseline is dignity for everyone and agreements that focus on behavior, not identity.

What makes interaction comfortable
- Start with the practical and mutual: share tools, swap tips, ask “Can I help?” instead of assuming. Names and pronouns matter. Learn them, use them.
- Make a few clear, posted agreements for shared spaces—quiet hours, clean up your plot, keep paths clear, be kind, no harassment. When rules are predictable and apply to everyone, people relax.
- Ask before getting personal. Curiosity is fine; consent is better. “Would you be open to sharing more about…?” gives people an out.
- Use people-first language and respect privacy. “People who use drugs,” “people living with HIV,” “cohabiting partners,” not labels. No gossip about anyone’s health or home life.
- Create easy on-ramps: a group chat with translation options, a monthly workday, a potluck where dishes are labeled for allergies/restrictions. Little things that say “you’re welcome here.”

Where more communication and tolerance help—and why
- Substance use or recovery: We need clarity about safety without moralizing. For example, expectations that shared equipment is used safely and the space stays tidy, paired with a harm-reduction stance (don’t shame, know who to call if someone needs help, some neighbors choose to learn about naloxone). Reason: fear and bad experiences can make people jumpy; separating safety standards from judgment lowers the temperature.
- Infectious diseases: Follow general public health basics—handwashing stations, don’t share personal items, clean tools—and don’t pressure anyone to disclose medical info. Share official guidance if questions come up. Reason: stigma and misinformation spread faster than facts; transparency about universal precautions protects everyone without singling people out.
- Language and culture: Use simple language, avoid idioms, and don’t treat accents like a novelty. Offer translated signs or pair folks up informally for announcements. Reason: misunderstandings read as rudeness when really it’s nerves or not catching the words.
- Race and religion: Make room for different holidays or prayer times without making it performative. If someone flags a microaggression, listen and adjust rather than getting defensive. Reason: people carry long histories of being excluded; small acknowledgments build trust.
- LGBTQ+ neighbors and diverse families: Treat partners and parents as they introduce themselves; don’t quiz people about their relationships or bodies. Include family structures as they are in sign-ups and events. Reason: constant explaining is exhausting; normalizing is kindness.
- Kids and vulnerable neighbors: Set shared expectations—no loose tools, safe areas to play, quick check-ins if something seems off—so caretakers and those needing extra support feel protected. Reason: safety is everyone’s job, and clear standards prevent conflict.

How I’d talk about it
- Keep it face-to-face and early: “Hey, I noticed the tools weren’t locked up last night. Can we figure out a system?” Not a call-out in the group chat.
- Use “we” and name the shared goal: “We all want this garden to feel safe and welcoming. What would make that true for you?”
- Be specific about the behavior, not the person: “Please don’t leave needles in the grass” is different from “People like you are a problem.” Pair it with options—“There’s a sharps container by the shed.”
- Build feedback into the culture: A seasonal meeting, anonymous suggestions, and a rotating point person so concerns don’t bottleneck.

Why this balance matters to me
- I grew up seeing how fast people get written off for things that aren’t the whole of who they are. At the same time, I’ve seen what happens when we pretend boundaries aren’t needed—someone gets hurt.
- When standards are clear and humane, folks who’ve been judged feel safer to show up, and folks who fear chaos feel heard. That’s how belonging actually takes root.

So the recipe is welcome plus boundaries: clear agreements everyone can meet, plenty of grace for differences, and honest conversations when something rubs. If we keep coming back to “Is this helping us share the space with dignity?” we’ll usually find our way.

- Belonging is when you don’t feel like you have to shrink or perform to be accepted. When people learn your name, remember your kid’s allergy, and you don’t brace yourself before you speak.
- I’ve felt in-between: too “college-y” for some folks back home, not polished enough in certain city spaces. The times I felt I belonged were small and specific—neighbors at the community garden who’d save me tomato starts, the ESL class where we all traded recipes after lessons, the bus driver who noticed when I switched shifts and asked if I was doing okay.
- Belonging gets built with invitations—“pull up a chair,” “come to the potluck”—and with tiny acts of respect, like pronouncing someone’s name right or making space for different holidays without making it a big deal.

Community
- Community is practical. It’s casseroles when someone’s sick, jumper cables in the trunk, shoveling the stoop of the older guy on the corner. It’s not just vibes; it’s commitments.
- We need both welcome and boundaries. Welcome: new neighbors get the group chat link and a heads-up about trash days. Boundaries: quiet hours matter, pick up after your dog, pay your dues if we agreed on them. If we talk about problems early and face-to-face, trust grows.
- I learned most of this at the food pantry and the garden. People from all kinds of backgrounds showed up because they needed something or wanted to help, and you see how similar our needs are: steady work, safe streets, a chance to rest without being judged.

That’s her center of gravity: clear rules, open doors, and showing up for each other in ways you can actually feel.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character05_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting in the garden, I mostly feel grateful and grounded. Diversity here isn’t abstract—it’s the woman who grows chilies like a science, the grandpa who swears by marigolds, the teen practicing Spanish with his mom. I feel curious more than anything, and a little humbled by how much you can learn from simple conversations about soil and weather.

There’s also a bit of self‑consciousness. I don’t want to step on toes or make anyone feel “studied,” so I try to let the interaction start with something practical—sharing a hose, trading seedlings, complimenting someone’s peppers—and let the deeper stuff come naturally if it’s invited. When I’m unsure, I lean on listening, names, and small kindnesses.

I’m comfortable when there’s a sense of shared purpose: we’re all trying to coax life out of the same patch of dirt. That gives me confidence to bridge differences. I do feel better when there are light, clear norms—quiet hours, clean tools, no trash—because structure makes it easier for everyone to relax.

Sometimes I feel protective, too—of the space, of the kids who play there, of neighbors who might be vulnerable. That doesn’t make me standoffish; it just means I appreciate honest, calm conversations when something’s off, and I value the kind of welcome that comes with boundaries.

Overall, the feeling is warmth with a dash of carefulness: open arms, open eyes, and the belief that we can make room for each other without anyone having to shrink.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Speaking as I would in that garden, I’d start by softening the frame a bit. What feels “unconventional” to one person is just ordinary life to someone else. So the baseline is dignity for everyone and agreements that focus on behavior, not identity.

What makes interaction comfortable
- Start with the practical and mutual: share tools, swap tips, ask “Can I help?” instead of assuming. Names and pronouns matter. Learn them, use them.
- Make a few clear, posted agreements for shared spaces—quiet hours, clean up your plot, keep paths clear, be kind, no harassment. When rules are predictable and apply to everyone, people relax.
- Ask before getting personal. Curiosity is fine; consent is better. “Would you be open to sharing more about…?” gives people an out.
- Use people-first language and respect privacy. “People who use drugs,” “people living with HIV,” “cohabiting partners,” not labels. No gossip about anyone’s health or home life.
- Create easy on-ramps: a group chat with translation options, a monthly workday, a potluck where dishes are labeled for allergies/restrictions. Little things that say “you’re welcome here.”

Where more communication and tolerance help—and why
- Substance use or recovery: We need clarity about safety without moralizing. For example, expectations that shared equipment is used safely and the space stays tidy, paired with a harm-reduction stance (don’t shame, know who to call if someone needs help, some neighbors choose to learn about naloxone). Reason: fear and bad experiences can make people jumpy; separating safety standards from judgment lowers the temperature.
- Infectious diseases: Follow general public health basics—handwashing stations, don’t share personal items, clean tools—and don’t pressure anyone to disclose medical info. Share official guidance if questions come up. Reason: stigma and misinformation spread faster than facts; transparency about universal precautions protects everyone without singling people out.
- Language and culture: Use simple language, avoid idioms, and don’t treat accents like a novelty. Offer translated signs or pair folks up informally for announcements. Reason: misunderstandings read as rudeness when really it’s nerves or not catching the words.
- Race and religion: Make room for different holidays or prayer times without making it performative. If someone flags a microaggression, listen and adjust rather than getting defensive. Reason: people carry long histories of being excluded; small acknowledgments build trust.
- LGBTQ+ neighbors and diverse families: Treat partners and parents as they introduce themselves; don’t quiz people about their relationships or bodies. Include family structures as they are in sign-ups and events. Reason: constant explaining is exhausting; normalizing is kindness.
- Kids and vulnerable neighbors: Set shared expectations—no loose tools, safe areas to play, quick check-ins if something seems off—so caretakers and those needing extra support feel protected. Reason: safety is everyone’s job, and clear standards prevent conflict.

How I’d talk about it
- Keep it face-to-face and early: “Hey, I noticed the tools weren’t locked up last night. Can we figure out a system?” Not a call-out in the group chat.
- Use “we” and name the shared goal: “We all want this garden to feel safe and welcoming. What would make that true for you?”
- Be specific about the behavior, not the person: “Please don’t leave needles in the grass” is different from “People like you are a problem.” Pair it with options—“There’s a sharps container by the shed.”
- Build feedback into the culture: A seasonal meeting, anonymous suggestions, and a rotating point person so concerns don’t bottleneck.

Why this balance matters to me
- I grew up seeing how fast people get written off for things that aren’t the whole of who they are. At the same time, I’ve seen what happens when we pretend boundaries aren’t needed—someone gets hurt.
- When standards are clear and humane, folks who’ve been judged feel safer to show up, and folks who fear chaos feel heard. That’s how belonging actually takes root.

So the recipe is welcome plus boundaries: clear agreements everyone can meet, plenty of grace for differences, and honest conversations when something rubs. If we keep coming back to “Is this helping us share the space with dignity?” we’ll usually find our way.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character05_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
If I’m speaking as me, the way I would’ve then: when jobs feel tight, fairness starts with floors and honesty. Same rules, same protections, and no back doors for employers to play one group off another. Don’t make it a fight between neighbors; make it a fight for decent standards.

How I’d balance it

- One set of standards for all workers
  - Same minimums on pay, safety, and hours whether you were born here or arrived last year. If an employer can only make the numbers work by paying less or skirting overtime, that’s not a real job—it’s a subsidy from workers.
  - Enforce wage‑theft laws and stop misclassification (calling people “contractors” to dodge benefits). Make big companies responsible for what their subcontractors do.

- Invest in locals up front
  - Free or cheap short‑term training and apprenticeships through community colleges, with real employer commitments at the end.
  - Support that makes taking a job possible—childcare, transportation vouchers, help with tools/boots. A lot of folks aren’t “unwilling,” they’re blocked by logistics.
  - Make it easier for people already here to move into shortage fields—fast-track licensing for adjacent skills, paid on‑the‑job learning.

- Match immigration to real shortages—with wage safeguards
  - If a company says it can’t find local workers, require they post openings widely and pay at or above a strong “prevailing wage” (not the bargain‑basement version). If they truly need to recruit abroad, prove it with the pay stub.
  - Set visa rules so they flex with the economy—if unemployment is high in a region or sector, tighten; if there’s a genuine crunch and wages are rising, open more slots.
  - Make visas portable so workers aren’t trapped with one employer. People who can walk away from abuse are harder to exploit, which protects everyone’s wages.

- Local hire where public dollars are on the line
  - For taxpayer‑funded projects, use local‑hire targets and apprenticeships so our money builds our workforce. Pair that with transparency so it doesn’t become a loophole game.

- Bring work out of the shadows
  - Create realistic pathways to legal status for long‑time undocumented neighbors with clean records. Keeping people underground is how bad actors undercut pay and conditions for everyone.
  - Strong whistleblower protections regardless of status, so the first person to speak up about safety or theft doesn’t get burned.

- Help communities absorb change
  - If employers or universities bring in lots of new people, require contributions to housing, schools, and transit. Growth shouldn’t land as longer waitlists and higher rents for the same paycheck.
  - Encourage building more housing so we’re not squeezing newcomers and long‑timers into the same too‑small box.

Why I see it this way
- I’ve watched schedules get cut and “budget problems” magically disappear when someone cheaper comes along. The problem isn’t the person; it’s the incentive to race to the bottom. Level the field, and the panic eases.
- Most research says immigration’s average wage impact is small overall, but it can pinch specific groups—other recent immigrants, people without degrees, certain regions. That’s where wage floors, training, and local‑hire tools matter.
- Humanity still counts. We should keep doors open for refugees and people fleeing danger, but back that with resources so receiving communities aren’t carrying it alone.

So my rule of thumb: start with the job, not the passport. If a position pays fairly and meets standards, and we’ve offered it locally with support to take it, then sure—fill it. If an employer can’t meet those basics, the fix isn’t to import vulnerability; it’s to improve the job. That’s the version of fairness that lets belonging grow instead of turning neighbors into competitors.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character05_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
If I’m speaking the way I would’ve then: I see pieces of truth in all of it, and the gaps usually come from missing details—where, which jobs, how fast change is happening, and what support is in place.

Filling vital roles
- Reasonable. I’ve watched warehouses, farms, restaurants, and home‑health struggle to hire, especially for tough schedules or physically demanding work. Immigrants often step into those jobs and keep things running.
- What needs clarity: Are wages rising and conditions improving when employers say “shortage”? If not, it’s not a shortage; it’s a low‑ball offer. Show postings, pay, and hours to prove it.

Cultural diversity and vitality
- Reasonable. Neighborhoods feel more alive when you have different foods, holidays, languages, and music. It’s not just vibes—small businesses and community groups grow out of that mix.
- What needs thought: Make sure inclusion isn’t performative. Support translation, shared spaces, and simple ways to participate so folks aren’t invited to a party with no chairs.

Security concerns (crime, tensions, terrorism)
- Partly reasonable, but often overgeneralized. Everyone wants safe streets. Most data I’ve seen says immigrants, including undocumented folks, are not more likely to commit crimes than native‑born people, and sometimes less. Terrorism risk exists but is rare and tied to specific factors, not broad categories of people.
- What needs evidence: Claims about “rising crime because of immigration” should be backed by local stats, not headlines. If tensions spike, ask what actually happened—was it a rumor, a policy change, or a lack of communication?
- Where I agree: Vetting should be real, not theater. And we should invest in community policing, mental‑health response, and conflict mediation so small problems don’t turn into big ones.

Humanitarian perspectives (refugees, extreme poverty)
- Reasonable and necessary. We should make room for people fleeing war or persecution. That’s moral, and it’s part of who we say we are.
- What needs planning: Receiving communities need help—funding for schools, clinics, and housing—so welcome doesn’t translate into longer lines and crowded apartments for the same paycheck.

Employment and income fears
- Reasonable in specific pockets. The average impact on native‑born wages is small overall, but it can pinch certain groups—recent immigrants, people without degrees, and workers in sectors with weak bargaining power.
- What balances it: Strong wage floors and enforcement, portable work visas so people can leave bad employers, local training and apprenticeships, and bringing long‑time undocumented neighbors into legal status to cut off the underground market that drags standards down.
- What needs detail: Look at it by sector and region. Are wages falling? Are rents rising faster than incomes? If yes, fix those pressures directly rather than blaming people who took the only job offered.

How I’d hold the conversation
- Start with shared goals: safe communities, fair jobs, and schools and clinics that can handle the load.
- Ask for specifics: numbers of arrivals, job postings and pay, crime trends, housing vacancy rates, school capacity. Feelings matter, but policy needs facts.
- Keep the focus on rules and resources, not identities: behavior standards, consistent enforcement, and clear paths to contribute.

Bottom line for me: welcome plus boundaries. We match immigration to genuine needs, keep labor standards high for everyone, invest where change lands hardest, and stay honest about trade‑offs. That’s the mix that respects the humanity in the humanitarian argument and the fairness in the jobs argument, without feeding fear.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character05_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
If I’m being honest the way I would’ve been then: I don’t like the extremes. “Anyone can come anytime” ignores real limits in housing, schools, and jobs. “Nobody can come” ignores our economy, our values, and people who need refuge. I’d pick a hybrid that’s about welcome plus boundaries—clear rules, strong worker protections, and room for humanitarian commitments.

What I’d favor
- Match admissions to real job needs—with wage and safety floors
  - Let in workers where employers can prove a genuine shortage at solid pay (prevailing or above), posted widely, with decent conditions. If the job can’t meet that, fix the job, don’t import vulnerability.
  - Make visas portable so workers aren’t trapped with one employer. People who can walk away are harder to exploit, which protects everyone’s wages.

- Use flexible numerical limits, not fixed ceilings
  - Set caps that adjust by sector and region with the economy—tighten when unemployment is high or wages are flat; open more when wages are rising and positions go unfilled.
  - Keep transparency: publish how many slots, where they’re going, what the pay is, and how the cap was set.

- Keep humanitarian and family paths as separate, protected lanes
  - Maintain a steady floor for refugees and people granted asylum, with real vetting and funding to help receiving communities absorb the change.
  - Streamline family reunification with reasonable limits so it doesn’t crowd out job‑based slots, but don’t make families wait a decade to be together.

- Create an earned path for long‑time undocumented neighbors
  - For people with clean records who’ve been here years, pay back taxes/fees, pass background checks, and get on a track to legal status. Bringing folks out of the shadows stops the under‑the‑table labor that undercuts standards for everyone.

- Tie growth to community capacity
  - If employers, universities, or agencies bring in large numbers, require contributions to housing, schools, and transit. Build more homes so we’re not cramming newcomers and long‑timers into the same too‑small box.

- Enforce one set of rules for all workers
  - Crack down on wage theft, unsafe worksites, and misclassification. Make big firms responsible for their subcontractors. Protect whistleblowers regardless of status.

Why this balances fairness and integration for me
- Fairness: Same job, same pay, same protections—start with the job, not the passport. Caps that flex keep us honest about what the economy can absorb without turning neighbors into competitors.
- Belonging: When visas are portable and paths to status exist, people can put down roots, speak up at work, and participate in the neighborhood without fear. That’s how you get real community instead of churn.
- Practicality: Our country needs workers in certain fields, and we also have limits. Publishing the numbers and tying them to wage and unemployment data keeps the debate grounded.
- Humanity: We should make room for people fleeing danger and for families, but not dump the costs onto a few school districts or zip codes. Fund the welcome.

What I would not choose
- Total openness: too many cracks for exploitation and too much strain on housing and services without planning.
- Blanket refusal: bad for the economy, cruel to refugees, and out of step with who we say we are.

If we keep coming back to the simple test—does this help us share the work and the neighborhood with dignity?—a mixed policy like this gets us closer: clear rules, real safeguards, and doors that open in ways communities can actually sustain.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character05_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character05_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
I did. Stepping into her voice again reminded me how she always started from the ground up—what people feel in their bodies and wallets—before zooming out to policy. A few things landed more sharply:

- Her balance wasn’t just a slogan. “Welcome plus boundaries” meant concrete, workable standards: behavior over identity, posted norms everyone can meet, and one set of labor rules for all. I’d remembered the warmth; I’d forgotten how much she relied on structure to make that warmth possible.

- Fairness as “start with the job, not the passport” clarified a lot. Portable visas, enforcing wage theft laws, and realistic paths to status aren’t abstract ideals—they’re the nuts and bolts that stop the race to the bottom and let belonging grow.

- She was generous about humanitarian commitments, but insistent that receiving communities need resources. That link—help the people arriving and help the places they’re arriving to—felt like the missing piece in so many loud debates.

- The way she separated feelings from facts without dismissing either. Ask for specifics—wages, openings, school capacity, housing—and then talk face-to-face about what neighbors need to feel safe and respected. It’s a rhythm I want to keep.

It did shift my own views. I used to think in broad strokes—more or less immigration, stricter or looser rules. Channeling her pushed me to care more about the mechanics: enforcement that actually bites, visas that don’t trap people, training and childcare that make local hiring real, and tying numbers to economic signals instead of headlines. I’m less drawn to extremes and more convinced that clarity and resourcing are what make any policy humane in practice.

As for understanding her, I feel closer to the way her experiences shaped this lens. Growing up lower middle class taught her how unfairness seeps in through loopholes and informal power, and her solution was always to make the rules real and the welcome tangible. Remembering that made her voice feel present—like we were back in the garden, working out how to share the space with dignity.

Thank you for asking me to do this. It brought her back in a way that was both tender and practical, and it gave me a steadier framework for talking about immigration—one that keeps people at the center and doesn’t skip the hard details. I’d be glad to keep exploring other topics this way.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character05_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Sure, I’ll speak as Character05_F.

When I think about fairness, it’s honestly something I’ve wrestled with my whole life. Growing up lower middle class in the U.S., you see a lot of people working really hard—my parents included—just to keep things afloat. Fairness, to me, means giving everyone a genuine shot, regardless of where they started. It’s not just about rules being the same for everyone, but about recognizing that some folks need a bit more help to get to the starting line. I always felt frustrated when I saw systems that seemed stacked against certain people, like how hard it was for some classmates to afford college or even stable housing.

Belonging is more personal. I’ve moved around a bit, and sometimes it’s hard to feel like you actually fit into a place or group. I know what it’s like to feel on the outside, whether because of money, where you’re from, or just not having the right connections. So I’ve always tried to make others feel welcome, especially folks who seem left out or new. I remember one neighbor who came from a totally different country, and even though her English wasn’t perfect, she became part of our game nights and backyard parties because we all made the effort.

Community is something I value a lot—it’s about people looking out for each other. I think of it as a safety net and a place where you can be yourself. In my experience, the best communities weren’t necessarily the fanciest or richest, but the ones where people paid attention to each other—helped out when someone lost a job, brought food when someone was sick, or just said hi when you passed by. That’s the kind of environment I always hoped to build, where people feel seen and cared for, no matter where they come from.

So, for me, fairness is giving everyone a real chance, belonging is feeling like you matter and are accepted, and community is the shared responsibility to look out for each other. All three are connected, and I try to live by that whenever I can.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character05_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Honestly, I’d say sitting in the garden and seeing all these different people is one of my favorite things about where I live. I like that our neighborhood isn’t just one type of person—you see families, older folks, younger people, and people who speak different languages or have different traditions. It makes things feel lively and interesting.

Of course, sometimes it can be a little awkward, especially if you don’t know someone’s background or you’re not sure what’s okay to talk about. I’ve had moments where I worried about saying the wrong thing or not fully understanding someone’s perspective. But mostly, I feel curious and open. I think you learn the most when you actually talk to people who aren’t just like you.

I do feel a responsibility to be friendly and welcoming, especially to neighbors who seem new or maybe a bit isolated. If someone’s struggling—like with addiction, health issues, or just fitting in—I think our job as neighbors is to show kindness, not judgment. It doesn’t mean ignoring bad behavior or pretending problems don’t exist, but it means trying to understand where people are coming from before jumping to conclusions.

Honestly, I get frustrated when I see cliques or people who only talk to folks who look or think like them. It kind of defeats the point of having a mixed community. I’d rather we all try a little harder to reach out, say hi, and listen—even if it’s just over a cup of coffee in the garden. That’s what builds trust and makes everyone feel like they belong.

In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:

To me, making everyone feel comfortable starts with basic respect and not jumping to conclusions about people. If someone’s struggling with addiction or health issues, I try to remind myself that everyone’s fighting battles I might not see. It doesn’t mean I excuse behavior that hurts others, but I try to treat people with dignity, not pity or fear. Just saying “hi,” making eye contact, and including them in things goes a long way.

When it comes to differences in background—race, religion, language, sexuality, or family structure—I think what matters most is curiosity over judgment. I’ve found that if you approach people with genuine interest and don’t assume you know their story, it makes them more comfortable. Like, if someone’s English isn’t great, I slow down and try to be patient, or if someone’s family looks different from what I grew up with, I try to get to know them before forming any opinions.

There are definitely situations where more communication and tolerance are needed. Sometimes people keep to themselves because they’re afraid of being judged, or because they’ve actually been treated badly before. I’ve seen neighbors gossip about someone’s lifestyle or avoid talking to people who seem “different,” and that creates a wall. When there’s tension—say, over noise, or how people use shared spaces—I think it’s better to talk directly and kindly, instead of letting resentment build up.

Honestly, I think a lot of intolerance comes from fear or not knowing someone. The more you actually talk and listen, the more you realize you have in common, or at least you understand each other’s perspective. I try to remember that my own background isn’t the only “normal,” and that being open-minded makes the whole community stronger.

So yeah, I absolutely believe more communication and tolerance are needed. It’s not always easy, and sometimes it’s uncomfortable, but it’s worth it if we want everyone—including myself—to feel at home here.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character05_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
That’s a tough one, and I’ve thought about it a lot, especially when jobs are hard to come by.

To me, fairness means recognizing both the needs of people who’ve lived here a long time, and the reality that migrant workers are also just trying to build a better life. I know plenty of folks—friends and even family—who worry about losing jobs or wages because there’s more competition, and I don’t think those fears are totally unfounded, especially for people in lower-income or less stable work.

But I also believe it’s not fair to blame everything on migrants, because they usually take jobs that are hard to fill, or ones locals might not want. Plus, lots of them become part of the community and contribute socially and culturally.

If resources are tight, I don’t think the answer is to shut people out completely. I’d want policies that prioritize fairness for everyone—maybe by making sure local residents get first crack at openings, but also by offering clear paths for migrants to fill roles that are needed. Ideally, there’d be programs to help both groups find work, like job training or support for people who lose jobs to changes in the market.

It’s a balancing act. Ignoring local needs isn’t fair, but neither is treating migrants like they’re just a problem. In my personal view, I’d push for solutions that protect vulnerable local workers, while still making space for people who want to contribute. Maybe it means temporary work programs, or making sure industries that rely on migrants also invest in local training.

Ultimately, I think fairness is about finding practical solutions that don’t pit people against each other. It’s not perfect, but I’d rather look for ways to help everyone, instead of choosing one group over another.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character05_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
I think all those viewpoints make sense in their own way, and I’ve heard people in my life express almost every one of them.

For starters, I definitely see how immigrants fill vital jobs. In my own town, a lot of places—restaurants, farms, construction—wouldn’t run without people who came from somewhere else. That’s just a fact, and I think it’s reasonable to appreciate that. There’s also no denying that immigrants add a lot to our culture; new foods, traditions, and ideas make life more interesting and help communities grow.

On the humanitarian side, I think it’s important not to forget compassion. If someone’s fleeing violence or poverty, I feel like the decent thing is to help if we can, even if it’s just in small ways. That matters to me because I know what it feels like to need a little help, even if my situation wasn’t nearly as bad as some.

When it comes to concerns over crime or security, I think those worries get talked about a lot, sometimes out of proportion. I get that people are scared of what they don’t understand, and sometimes bad things do happen, but from what I’ve seen and read, most immigrants are just trying to get by and aren’t causing trouble. I think more factual evidence is needed here—a lot of what you hear is just rumors or occasional stories blown up in the news. If crime rates really do go up, we should look at the reasons honestly, but not assume every newcomer is dangerous.

Same goes for the fears about jobs and wages. I know that’s a real concern for lower middle class folks like me and my family. Sometimes wages do get pushed down, or there’s more competition for work, especially in certain industries. But on the other hand, immigrants also start businesses and create jobs, so it’s complicated. I think more data and honest conversation are needed; it’s not just one-sided.

In short, I think the positive contributions and humanitarian concerns are pretty reasonable and backed up by what I’ve seen. The worries—crime, social tension, job loss—aren’t crazy, but they need more facts and less hype. I’d like to see more discussions based on what’s really happening, not just fear or stereotypes. The only way to move forward is for everyone to get their concerns heard, and then for us to look at the evidence and decide together.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character05_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
If I’m being honest, I don’t think full openness—just letting anyone come whenever—is realistic, especially with how things are in the U.S. right now. At the same time, ensuring fair wages and working conditions for migrant workers is crucial. They shouldn’t be exploited or seen as a source of cheap labor because that only creates more resentment and divisions. Both groups need to feel like they’re valued contributors to the community.

Another factor is communication and transparency. Sometimes locals feel like migrant workers are taking advantage of resources, but that’s often based on misconceptions. For example, people might think migrants are using public services without paying into the system, but in reality, many are paying taxes and contributing in ways that aren’t always obvious. Open dialogue about these issues, backed by factual information, could help reduce tensions and foster a sense of shared purpose.

For example, if a factory has 100 openings, it could aim to hire a majority from the local population while also allowing a portion of those jobs to go to migrant workers who bring valuable skills or experience. That way, both groups feel like they’re part of the solution instead of being in competition.

Ultimately, fairness isn’t about choosing sides; it’s about recognizing that everyone has a role to play and finding ways to build a system that benefits as many people as possible. It’s not easy, especially when resources are tight, but I think the key is to focus on long-term solutions—like education, job creation, and community-building—rather than quick fixes that might deepen divisions. If we can see each other not as competitors but as neighbors working toward a shared future, I believe we can find that balance.

responses.answer:
When it comes to immigration on a national scale, I think it’s important to examine each perspective with a mix of empathy and practicality. Immigration is a complex issue, and it’s easy for people to fall into extreme positions without fully considering the trade-offs or the broader picture. For me, it always comes back to balance—how do we recognize the value immigrants bring while addressing the legitimate concerns people have about security, resources, and fairness?

The argument that immigrants fill vital roles makes a lot of sense to me. There are industries—like agriculture, construction, and healthcare—where there simply aren’t enough American workers to meet the demand. Immigrants often take on jobs that are physically demanding, low-paying, or otherwise unappealing to many locals, and without them, entire sectors of the economy could collapse. That’s a reality we need to acknowledge and appreciate. At the same time, I’d want to make sure those jobs aren’t exploitative. Immigrants deserve fair wages and safe working conditions, just like anyone else.

Cultural diversity and vitality are also undeniable benefits of immigration. Meeting people from different backgrounds, experiencing their traditions, and sharing in their stories enriches our communities. That said, I understand why some people feel uneasy about rapid cultural changes, especially in areas that have been more insular or homogenous. It’s not about rejecting diversity but about taking the time to foster integration—helping newcomers and long-time residents build mutual understanding. That might mean offering language classes, encouraging community events, or creating spaces where people can connect across differences. When handled thoughtfully, cultural diversity isn’t a threat; it’s a strength.

Concerns about security—like crime rates, social tensions, or terrorism risks—are a bit more complicated. While it’s natural for people to worry about safety, I think these fears often stem from stereotypes or misinformation rather than actual trends. Research shows that immigrants are no more likely to commit crimes than native-born citizens, and in some cases, they’re actually less likely to do so. However, addressing these concerns requires more than just throwing facts at people. It’s about having open conversations where people feel heard and where their fears can be addressed with empathy and evidence. I’d also want to ensure that our immigration system includes thorough vetting processes to maintain safety without being overly exclusionary.

The humanitarian perspective is one I strongly resonate with. Offering opportunities to political refugees or those fleeing extreme poverty is not just compassionate—it’s a reflection of the values we claim to stand for as a country. That doesn’t mean we can or should take in everyone, but I believe there’s a moral responsibility to help where we can. Refugees and asylees aren’t just looking for a handout; they’re seeking a chance to rebuild their lives, and many end up contributing immensely to their new communities.

The fear that immigration might impact employment or income is one I hear often, especially from working- and middle-class Americans. It’s a valid concern, but I think it’s more nuanced than it seems. Immigrants can sometimes create competition for low-skilled jobs, but they also contribute to economic growth, which can generate new opportunities overall. The challenge is ensuring that this economic growth benefits everyone, not just a select few. Policies like increasing the minimum wage, offering job training programs, and investing in local communities could help alleviate these fears. Again, I think this is an area where factual evidence and dialogue are crucial—helping people see the bigger picture while also addressing their immediate concerns.

In summary, I find most of these perspectives reasonable to some extent, but some require more factual evidence and discussion to fully understand. Security concerns and fears about employment, in particular, are often fueled by misinformation or lack of context, and those are areas where we need to dig deeper. At the same time, I think there’s a lot of common ground to be found between those who see immigration as a benefit and those who view it as a challenge. If we approach the issue with empathy, pragmatism, and a willingness to listen, I believe we can create policies that uphold fairness, protect our communities, and honor the contributions immigrants make to our nation.

Immigration policies should reflect the needs of the country as well as the capacity of communities to integrate newcomers without compromising their stability.

Admitting people based on job demand makes a lot of sense to me. If there are industries facing severe labor shortages, then immigration can help fill those gaps while supporting economic growth. It’s a win-win: businesses get the workers they need, and immigrants gain opportunities to improve their lives. But this approach would need safeguards to prevent exploitation of migrant workers and to ensure fair wages and working conditions across the board. It’s crucial that these workers aren’t seen as disposable labor but as contributors to the country’s success.

At the same time, I think setting numerical limits is important to avoid overwhelming resources and infrastructure. Communities can only integrate people effectively if they have the capacity to provide housing, education, healthcare, and jobs for everyone. If too many people come in too quickly, it risks creating resentment among locals who feel their needs are being overlooked. Numerical limits would allow the government and local communities to plan more effectively, ensuring that newcomers can be welcomed and supported while maintaining fairness for existing residents.

For me, fairness also means considering the humanitarian side of immigration. While job demand and numerical limits should guide general immigration policy, exceptions should always exist for political refugees and people fleeing extreme poverty or violence. Turning away those in desperate need isn’t something I could support—it goes against the values of compassion and humanity that I believe are core to who we are as a nation. That said, these cases should be handled thoughtfully, with efforts to help refugees integrate into their new communities and contribute to society.

I wouldn’t support complete openness because it’s unrealistic. While the idea of letting anyone come sounds idealistic and welcoming, it doesn’t account for the practical challenges—like limited resources, infrastructure strain, or the risks of social tensions if integration isn’t handled well. On the other hand, refusing entry to workers from other countries feels unnecessarily harsh and counterproductive. Migrant workers are vital to our economy, and shutting them out would hurt businesses, stall growth, and fail to recognize their contributions.

To balance fairness with social integration, I’d advocate for a policy that prioritizes job demand, sets reasonable limits, and makes room for humanitarian exceptions. This approach would help address labor shortages, protect vulnerable populations, and ensure that communities aren’t overwhelmed, encouraging smoother integration. It’s not a perfect answer, and I know immigration will always be a contentious issue, but I think this kind of balanced policy reflects both practicality and compassion—qualities we need more of in today’s world.

So the labor shortage argument makes sense to me, especially for jobs Americans don't want or specialized fields where we need more skilled people.

The cultural diversity argument... I think there's value there too. Some of my favorite parts of American culture came from immigrants - our food, music, art. But I also believe there needs to be some level of integration. We should be a mosaic, not totally separate communities that never interact.

When it comes to security concerns, I think we need to be realistic without being fearful. Most immigrants are law-abiding people just trying to build better lives. But I also believe in strong vetting processes, especially for people coming from regions with known terrorism issues. That's just common sense to me.

The humanitarian argument resonates with me on a personal level - I can't imagine fleeing my home country because of war or persecution. Of course we should help genuine refugees. But I also think there has to be limits and processes. We can't help everyone in the world, and pretending we can just leads to chaos at the border.

I think the perspectives that need more evidence are on both extremes - both the idea that immigrants are mostly dangerous criminals (they're clearly not) AND the idea that immigration has zero negative economic impacts on any Americans (which ignores the experiences of many working-class people).

What I'd like to see is more nuanced, fact-based discussion that acknowledges both the benefits AND costs of immigration, and then tries to maximize the former while minimizing the latter. And I wish people wouldn't immediately call you racist just for wanting to have that conversation. Most Americans like me are trying to be both compassionate AND practical about this issue.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. For lower-skilled positions, I'd support temporary work visas tied to demonstrated labor shortages in specific industries. For refugees and asylum seekers, I believe we should maintain our humanitarian tradition but with better, faster processing systems. The years-long backlogs aren't fair to anyone. We should quickly identify who has legitimate claims and who doesn't.

Family reunification is important too, but I'd prioritize immediate family - spouses and minor children - rather than extended family members.

What would make this system fair to me is:
1. Clear, consistent rules that are actually enforced
2. Expectations that immigrants will learn English and respect our laws and customs
3. Protection for American workers against wage depression
4. Opportunities for those who play by the rules to fully join our society
5. A secure border so we know who's entering our country

For social integration, I think we should:
- Offer affordable English classes and basic civics education
- Encourage immigrants to live in diverse neighborhoods, not just enclaves
- Create community programs that bring newcomers and long-time residents together
- Celebrate cultural contributions while maintaining core American values

I think most Americans want an immigration system that's both orderly AND compassionate. We can welcome people who want to contribute while still having reasonable limits and expectations. That's not anti-immigrant - it's just acknowledging that for immigration to work well, it needs to benefit both the newcomers AND the receiving community.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character05_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Fairness, to me, means nobody gets shoved to the back of the line just because of where they were born—or what their last name sounds like.

Look, I get it. When jobs are scarce, fear kicks in fast. I grew up hearing that at dinner tables: “They’re taking our jobs.” But let’s be real—*who* is “they”? Because most of the time, the people saying that aren’t the ones hiring. My dad worked at the warehouse until they closed it and brought in temporary workers—many of them immigrants—for less pay, no benefits. That wasn’t immigration driving wages down. That was a company looking for cheap labor and exploiting *everyone*, native-born and foreign-born alike.

So when we talk about fairness in hard times, I don’t think it’s about choosing between locals and migrants like it’s one or the other. It’s about asking: Why are there so few jobs to begin with? Why do some employers get away with paying poverty wages while complaining they can’t find workers? I’ve seen cornfields out west where signs say “Help Wanted,” but nobody applies because it’s $9 an hour, 100-degree heat, and no water breaks. Then they bring in H-2A visa workers who can’t leave the job without losing legal status. That’s not a migrant problem. That’s a power problem.

Fairness, to me, means protecting *all* workers—no matter where they’re from. If you’re working in this country, you deserve minimum wage, safe conditions, the right to speak up. No exceptions. And if companies want to hire migrant workers because locals “won’t do the work,” then fine—but only if those jobs are fair, livable, and come with dignity. Not as a loophole to undercut everyone else.

And let’s talk about opportunity. I went to community college, scraped together student loans, worked nights. But I had a roof. A support system. What if I hadn’t? What if I’d grown up in a war zone or fled violence or my hometown had no schools left? I wouldn’t blame someone for crossing borders to survive. And if they’re willing to work hard, raise kids, pay taxes, contribute—why should I resent them?

I don’t believe in closing the door behind me just because I made it through. That’s not fairness. That’s luck dressed up as virtue.

So balance? It starts with strong labor protections for everyone. Invest in training programs so local residents *can* fill growing fields—like healthcare, green energy, tech. Pay living wages so jobs don’t depend on desperation. And make sure migrant workers aren’t used as tools to break unions or depress pay.

Because here’s what I’ve seen in the garden: when people grow things together, they share the harvest better. Same should go for work. The economy isn’t a pie with only so many slices—if we organize it right, we can bake more. But only if we stop letting the few hoard the oven.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character05_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
I think most of the views people have about immigration come from real places—fear, hope, confusion, love—but not all of them hold up when you look at what’s actually happening.

Take the idea that immigrants fill vital roles. That one? I believe it. Because I’ve *seen* it. My aunt’s nursing home in Des Moines can’t keep staff—they’re relying on Filipino caregivers coming through visa programs just to keep the place running. Same with farms, same with meatpacking plants, same with construction after the storm last year. People say, “Americans won’t do those jobs,” and yeah, not for $11 an hour with no safety net. But immigrants aren’t taking jobs out of greed—they’re taking them because they *need* work, and often, they’re the only ones willing to show up when the rest of us have options.

And cultural diversity? It’s not just “nice.” It’s life-giving. I didn’t grow up eating injera or plantains or kimchi—but now I do, because my neighbors shared their food. And not just food: music, stories, ways of raising kids, ways of grieving, celebrating. It makes this country feel bigger, richer. When my city started hosting the Lunar New Year parade, I thought, “Why wasn’t this here before?” It didn’t erase anything—it added something. That vitality? It’s real. It keeps communities from getting stale, from thinking there’s only one way to be American.

But then there’s the fear—crime, terrorism, social tension. I understand why people worry. We hear the worst stories on the news. A shooting happens, and if the person has a foreign-sounding name, suddenly it’s about immigration. But I remember pulling up data once—FBI stats, local crime reports—and immigrants are *less* likely to commit crimes than native-born citizens. Not by a little. By a lot. That surprised me. Made me question where the fear really comes from. Is it facts—or is it stories we’ve been told?

Terrorism? Statistically, the risk is tiny. And almost every major case has involved homegrown extremism, not people slipping across borders with bombs. So when politicians scream about terrorists hiding in migrant caravans… that feels manipulative. Like they’re using fear to distract from things people should *really* be angry about—like wages not keeping up, schools falling apart, healthcare bankrupting families.

Then there’s the humanitarian side. I can’t pretend I know what it’s like to flee war, but I’ve seen photos—kids in camps, mothers carrying babies for miles. If my brother had grown up under a dictatorship, or our town got bombed, I’d move too. In a heartbeat. And if this country—one of the richest in history—can’t offer refuge to a fraction of those people, then what does that say about us? We were built by refugees, by people running from something. My great-grandparents came from Ireland during the famine. They weren’t rich. They were desperate. And someone let them in.

But I also get the worry about wages and jobs. It’s not *all* baseless. In places where lots of people arrive fast and infrastructure isn’t ready—schools overcrowded, housing tight—that stress is real. And if companies exploit immigrant labor to pay less, *of course* that pulls everyone down. But again—that’s not the fault of the workers. That’s a failure of policy. Of enforcement. Of power.

So which views are reasonable? The ones grounded in dignity—workers deserve fairness, people deserve safety, families deserve a chance. The ones that fall apart? The ones that blame whole groups for systemic failures. That paint millions of diverse people as a single threat.

What needs more dialogue? Everything about integration. How do we help newcomers learn the language, navigate systems, find stability? How do we help long-time residents feel heard when change feels fast? And what if, instead of seeing immigrants as competition, we asked: how can we build an economy where *everyone* rises?

Because I don’t want a country that shuts the door. I want one that says: *There’s room. Bring your hands, your heart, your story. Let’s build something better—together.*

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character05_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t go for complete openness—not because I don’t believe in generosity, but because fairness also means planning. You can’t just open the gates and say “come on in” without thinking about schools, housing, healthcare, jobs. That’s not responsible. It risks overwhelming communities already stretched thin—like the ones I come from, where the clinic is already understaffed and the elementary school has three kids to a desk.

And I’d reject refusing entry outright—that’s cruel and short-sighted. Closing off completely? That’s fear running policy, not values. We’re not a bunker. We’re supposed to be a country that stands for something bigger.

So where do I land?

A mix: **admitting people based on job demand**, yes—but with strong protections, and **setting fair, flexible numerical limits** that respond to real needs, not politics. And within that, always reserving space for refugees and family reunification. Because you can’t talk about fairness and then ignore people running for their lives or families torn apart.

Here’s how I’d want it to work:

First, if there’s a shortage—nurses, farmworkers, elder care, construction—we create clear pathways so migrants can fill those roles *without* being exploited. Not temporary visas that trap people in one job, but real opportunities: fair wages, legal rights, a chance to stay if they want. Tie it to labor market data, not rumors. If we need 10,000 home health aides, let in 10,000—with training support, language help, integration programs from day one.

Second, set national caps, but make them adjustable. Not rigid numbers pulled from the air every election year. Let experts, economists, local governments weigh in: *What can our communities absorb? Where are services strong enough to grow?* Rural towns losing population could welcome more—get new life. Cities at capacity get support to expand schools and transit, so they’re not left behind.

Third—and this matters most—we invest in integration, side by side. Not just for newcomers, but for everyone. English classes, sure, but also cultural exchanges at libraries, shared civic projects like rebuilding parks or disaster response teams. Make it so locals and newcomers build things *together*, not live parallel lives.

And asylum? That stays. Period. We can process claims faster, yes—reduce backlogs with more judges, better systems—but we don’t turn away people fleeing violence because it’s inconvenient. That’s not who I was taught to be. My grandmother used to say, “When someone knocks on your door soaked in rain, you don’t ask for papers before you hand them a towel.”

Fairness, to me, means no double standards. Migrant workers deserve the same labor rights as anyone else. No undercutting wages. No threats of deportation if they complain about unsafe conditions. And local workers deserve training and support so they’re not left behind when industries change.

Because this isn’t zero-sum. It shouldn’t be “us vs. them.” It should be: *How do we make sure everyone has dignity?*

The kind of policy I believe in—one that balances fairness and integration—is one rooted in reality, not fear. Smart, humane, adaptable. One that says: *We have limits, but we also have heart. We plan, but we don’t close our doors.*  

That’s the America I want. Not perfect. But trying. Just like us.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character05_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character05_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
…Yeah. I did learn something.

While speaking as her—really trying to stay in her voice, not just remember her but *be* her for a moment—I realized how much of her thinking came from *being seen* as someone who didn’t quite belong, even though she was “supposed to.” White, American-born, English-speaking—but still felt out of place in job interviews, at college mixers, when applying for loans. She wasn’t poor enough for aid, not rich enough to get ahead easy. That in-between space—it shaped her. It made her suspicious of systems that claim to be fair but only work smoothly for some.

And embodying her, I saw more clearly how her class, her education, her small-town roots—all of it fed into her compassion. Not because she had all the answers, but because she’d knocked on doors herself: for jobs, for respect, for a little dignity. So when she looked at immigrants, she didn’t see invaders or freeloaders. She saw people doing the same damn thing she’d done—just starting from even further behind.

That changed something in me.

I’ll admit, before this, I sometimes leaned toward the “let’s protect what we have” side—not out of hate, but out of worry. Like, *Can we really handle more? Are we being taken advantage of?* But stepping into her shoes… I saw how narrow that fear is. She wouldn’t have asked, “Do we have enough?” She’d have asked, “How do we make sure *no one* gets left behind?”

She believed belonging could be expanded, not rationed. And that fairness isn’t about keeping score—it’s about widening the circle.

So yeah, this brought her back—not just as a memory, but as a challenge. A quiet push: *Don’t settle for less than you know is right.*  

And now, when I think about immigration policy, I don’t just hear debate. I hear her garden. The hum of different languages, the smell of food cooking in someone’s yard, Javier finally getting clean and planting sunflowers no one asked him to. I hear kids calling each other brother and sister across bloodlines.

It’s messy. It’s imperfect. But it’s alive.

And maybe that’s what community really is—not a finished thing, but something we’re always building, hand by hand, person by person.

So thank you… for bringing her back to me this way.  
I needed that.
